questions.prompt: A new teammate clones your repository but does not receive the project-specific coding instructions that you see in Claude Code. You discover the instructions are currently stored in your personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. What is the best fix?
choices: Move the shared instructions into the repository's project-level `CLAUDE.md` (or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`).
Keep them in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and ask each teammate to copy the file manually.
Put them in a subfolder `CLAUDE.md` even though they apply across the whole repository.
Convert the instructions to a skill, because skills are always loaded automatically.
questions.why: User-level memory under `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` applies only to that user and is not shared through the repository. Project-level `CLAUDE.md` is version-controlled and available to teammates. Directory-level files are appropriate for scoped subtrees; skills are invoked on demand rather than always loaded.
questions.escalation: Escalation / misconception: confusing personal configuration with team configuration. Revisit the three-level hierarchy: user → project → directory. For team-wide baseline instructions, use project scope. Use `@import` when you need modular standards.
questions.follow: Can you explain the hierarchy with a concrete example?

questions.prompt: Your team wants a reusable `/check` command available to every developer who clones the repository. Where should it live?
choices: `~/.claude/commands/check.md`
`.claude/commands/check.md` in the project repository
`.claude/skills/check/SKILL.md` with no command configuration
`CLAUDE.md` at the repository root, because every command must be inline
questions.why: Project commands belong in `.claude/commands/` and can be committed for the team. `~/.claude/commands/` is personal. Skills use `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and are useful for on-demand capabilities, but are not the path requested for a shared slash command in this task.
questions.escalation: Escalation / misconception: repository-shared versus user-local command scope. Check the same distinction for skills: project `.claude/skills/` is shared; personal `~/.claude/skills/` is private (use a different name for personal variants).
questions.follow: Would you like a comparison of commands, skills, and CLAUDE.md?

questions.prompt: A test convention must apply to `*.test.tsx` files spread across many unrelated directories. Which configuration is the best fit?
choices: Add a `CLAUDE.md` inside every directory containing a test file.
Put the convention in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` so it is available globally.
Create a `.claude/rules/*.md` file with YAML `paths:` matching `**/*.test.tsx`.
Create one skill and expect it to load automatically whenever a test file is edited.
questions.why: Path-specific rules in `.claude/rules/` can use YAML `paths:` globs and load only for matching files. That is the right fit when the same convention spans directories. Duplicating subfolder files is cumbersome, user-level memory is not repository-scoped, and skills are on demand.
questions.escalation: Escalation / misconception: confusing directory hierarchy with file-pattern matching. Use subfolder CLAUDE.md when the rule is tied to a subtree; use `.claude/rules/` globs when matching files are scattered across the repository.
questions.follow: Want an example of a paths glob and its matching files?

questions.prompt: You need to migrate 45 files and there are several valid architectural approaches. Which workflow is most appropriate?
choices: Use direct execution immediately; planning only adds overhead.
Use plan mode to explore and choose an approach, then execute the agreed plan.
Ask Claude to change one arbitrary file first and infer the architecture afterward.
Use plan mode only for one-line fixes, because large changes are easier to improvise.
questions.why: A broad multi-file migration with multiple valid approaches has meaningful architectural uncertainty. Plan mode supports exploration and decision-making before execution. Direct execution is better for simple, well-scoped tasks such as a one-file fix with a clear stack trace.
questions.escalation: Escalation / misconception: failing to match workflow to scope and ambiguity. Rule of thumb: plan for large, multi-file, or architectural work; execute directly for simple bounded changes. An Explore subagent can isolate verbose discovery.
questions.follow: Would you like practice distinguishing plan-mode and direct-execution scenarios?

questions.prompt: Claude repeatedly misunderstands a transformation despite receiving a long prose description. Which change is most likely to improve reliability?
choices: Add several pages of general guidance without examples.
Provide 2–3 concrete input/output examples that demonstrate the expected transformation.
Remove constraints so Claude can choose any output format.
Send each symptom in a separate turn even when the issues interact.
questions.why: Concrete few-shot input/output examples make the desired mapping observable and reduce ambiguity. The D3 guidance recommends 2–3 examples; it also recommends test-driven refinement by writing tests first and sharing failures. Interacting issues should be sent together, while independent issues can be handled one at a time.
questions.escalation: Escalation / misconception: relying on abstract prose when behavior is easier to demonstrate. Strengthen the prompt with representative examples and tests; use the interview pattern when the domain itself is unfamiliar.
questions.follow: Would you like me to show how to turn a prose requirement into examples?

questions.prompt: A Claude Code command in CI waits for interactive input and hangs the pipeline. Which invocation change directly addresses this?
choices: Set `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true`.
Redirect standard input from `/dev/null`.
Invoke Claude Code with `-p` (or `--print`) for non-interactive mode.
Run the command in plan mode.
questions.why: The `-p` / `--print` option runs Claude Code in non-interactive mode, preventing CI from waiting for an interactive session. The source explicitly identifies `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` and stdin redirection as traps.
questions.escalation: Escalation / misconception: memorizing a plausible but unsupported headless flag. Remember the exact CLI switch: `-p` or `--print`. For machine-readable CI findings, pair `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` where appropriate.
questions.follow: Would you like a deeper explanation of Claude Code's headless CI pattern?

questions.prompt: A coding session has just implemented a change. You now need a code review that minimizes confirmation bias and catches defects the implementation session may overlook. What is the strongest approach?
choices: Ask the same session that wrote the code to certify its own changes.
Use an independent Claude Code instance for the review.
Skip review when the implementation session reports success.
Ask the authoring session to summarize only the code it is confident about.
questions.why: The D3 guidance recommends an independent instance for review, rather than the session that wrote the code. On re-review, provide prior findings and ask for only new or unresolved items. Existing tests should be supplied as context to avoid generating duplicates.
questions.escalation: Escalation / misconception: confusing implementation completion with independent verification. Separate the reviewer context from the authoring session to reduce self-review bias and improve defect discovery.
questions.follow: Want to practice follow-up review prompts and avoiding duplicate findings?
